what: Kernel #1 pass 4: the hardware ceiling vs our kernel, measured on the same card
method: Dense fp32 GEMV with no dequant reads a known number of bytes with the same launch pattern and reports GB/s. Persistent NVFP4 kernel loops 128, 512 and 1024 times inside one launch so DVFS sees sustained load.

conclusion.headline: The card sustains 244 GB/s. Our kernel gets 22 GB/s at the same moment on the same hardware. The gap is 11x and it belongs to the kernel, not to throttling, DVFS or the machine.
conclusion.why_this_settles_the_earlier_questions: Pass 3 measured 585 MHz median and blamed throttling. That was a real observation but the wrong explanation for the bandwidth gap: a dense kernel in the same environment reaches 76% of peak, so the clock was never the limiting factor for a memory-bound kernel that is actually efficient. Persistent launches also did nothing (22.4 -> 21.7 GB/s), which rules out launch overhead and DVFS wake-up as the cause.
conclusion.so_the_cause_is_in_the_kernel: At 22 GB/s the kernel is dominated by its own work per byte: the FP4 decode and the scale decode are done per element inside the K loop, and the tile is narrow (BLOCK_N=64 with a 3D comparison-free but still scalar-heavy decode). The dense kernel proves memory can be fed fast; ours cannot consume it.

measured_vs_target.position: 15% of target, 9% of the measured ceiling.

caveats: The clock sampler returned empty for every run, so this pass has bandwidth without clock telemetry. Pass 3's clock data stands as the last clock evidence.

The dense kernel is fp32 and coalesced; the NVFP4 kernel reads 4-bit packed data and decodes per element. Some of the 11x gap is inherent to sub-byte formats, but not all of it: a well written FP4 dequant should sit far closer to the dense number than 9%.
next_levers_ranked_by_expected_gain: Decode once per 16-value scale block and reuse across a wider BLOCK_N, so the decode cost is amortised instead of per element.
Stage scales in shared memory: they are read per element today and are 1 byte per 16, so the same scale is reloaded 16x.
Load packed nibbles as 128-bit vectors (attempted in pass 2 but that run could not be trusted because of the clock noise now explained).
Raise BLOCK_N so each program streams more contiguous bytes per scale.
